title: Bioinformatics
description: Biological databases and tools, searching the biomedical literature, sequence alignment and homology, alignment scoring and methods, and a basic introduction to Linux for bioinformatics work.

topics.title: Biological Databases and Tools
topics.summary: Biological databases organise data such as nucleotide and protein sequences, genomes, structures, genetic variation and gene expression, in primary and secondary forms. Tools such as Entrez, BLAST, FASTA and Clustal search and compare that data, mostly through NCBI and EMBL-EBI.
subtopics: Types of database: public or private, generalised or specialised, curated or not
Nucleotide databases: GenBank, EMBL-EBI, DDBJ (INSDC); RefSeq, UniGene
Protein databases: PIR, SWISS-PROT, TrEMBL; PROSITE, Pfam
Genome, structural (PDB, CATH, SCOP), variation (dbSNP) and expression (GEO) databases
Tools: Entrez, BLAST, FASTA, Dotplot, Clustal, EMBOSS
Resources: NCBI and EMBL-EBI

topics.title: Information Search and Retrieval
topics.summary: Searching the literature is an essential and often difficult part of research, made easier by resources such as PubMed, eBlast, Google Scholar, Scopus and ScienceDirect. PubMed searches are sharpened by breaking the question into keywords and using MeSH, the NLM's controlled vocabulary.
subtopics: Why literature searching matters
PubMed and MEDLINE
eBlast, Google Scholar, Scopus, ScienceDirect
Why use PubMed
Steps in a literature search
MeSH terms

topics.title: Sequence Alignment and Homology
topics.summary: Sequence alignment arranges two or more DNA, RNA or protein sequences, preserving their order, to show where they are similar and where they differ. Similarity can suggest shared function, structure and ancestry (homology), with orthologs arising from speciation and paralogs from gene duplication.
subtopics: What sequence alignment is; optimal alignment
Why align: function, structure, evolution, annotation
Mutations: insertion, deletion, substitution; gaps
Identity, similarity and homology
Orthologous and paralogous sequences
Pairwise, multiple, global and local alignment

topics.title: Alignment Scoring and Methods
topics.summary: An alignment is scored column by column, rewarding matches and penalising mismatches and gaps, using either distance scoring (lowest is best) or similarity scoring (highest is best). Alignments are found by brute force, dot plots, dynamic programming (Needleman–Wunsch, Smith–Waterman) or heuristics (BLAST, FASTA).
subtopics: Scoring schemes: substitution scores and gap penalties
Distance scoring and its use in phylogenetic trees
Similarity scoring and its use in database searching
Brute force and the dot matrix method
Dynamic programming: Needleman–Wunsch (global), Smith–Waterman (local)
Heuristic methods: BLAST and FASTA

topics.title: Multiple Sequence Alignment and Protein Structure Prediction
topics.summary: A multiple sequence alignment lines up three or more sequences to reveal conserved regions, and progressive methods such as Clustal build it along a guide tree. Protein structure is described at four levels and is determined experimentally or predicted by homology modelling, threading or ab initio methods.
subtopics: What MSA is and why it matters
Applications of MSA
Progressive alignment and its weaknesses; iterative and consistency-based methods
MSA tools: Clustal Omega, MUSCLE, MAFFT, T-Coffee
Four levels of protein structure; experimental methods
Homology modelling, threading and ab initio prediction

topics.title: Basic Introduction to Linux
topics.summary: Linux is a free, open-source clone of UNIX, used from a terminal running a shell such as Bash. Files sit in a hierarchy under the root /, reached by absolute or relative paths and managed with commands such as pwd, ls, cd, mkdir, rmdir, cp, mv and rm.
subtopics: UNIX and Linux; why Linux; distributions
The terminal and the shell (Bash)
The UNIX file system; home and working directory
Absolute and relative paths; ~, . and ..
Directory commands: pwd, ls, mkdir, cd, rmdir
File commands cp, mv, rm; shortcuts and man pages
